items.t: Texas Instruments stock targets connected factories with new chips
sum: Texas Instruments used the week to strengthen its industrial technology narrative. In a Nov. 3 release, Texas Instruments marked 70 years of operations in Europe and highlighted work with ABB Robotics, Porsche, Schneider Electric and Husqvarna Group.

The company linked those customer relationships to industrial automation, next-generation vehicles, AI data-center power systems and connected outdoor products. TI said its European presence is focused on helping customers develop more autonomous and AI-driven systems, while its portfolio covers analog and embedded processing applications.

On Nov. 5, TI announced the TICS100MOD multiprotocol communications system-on-module and the TIOM2212 dual-channel IO-Link master. The company release said the TICS100MOD supports EtherCAT, EtherNet/IP and Profinet on one piece of hardware. Engineers can switch protocols through firmware updates rather than redesigning the hardware.

The TIOM2212 connects sensors and actuators to higher-level Industrial Ethernet networks. Preproduction quantities of the IO-Link master are available now, while TI plans to make the communications module available by year-end 2026. The products are intended to reduce design complexity in factory automation, robotics and Industrial Internet of Things systems.

TI will present the new industrial communications technology at electronica in Munich from Nov. 10 to 13, including demonstrations in Hall C4, booth 159. For investors, the event offers a near-term window into how TI is positioning analog, embedded processing and connectivity products across industrial and AI-related applications.
Texas Instruments stock traded at 248.85 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 11:24 CET on Saturday, November 7, 2026. The real-time quote of Texas Instruments stock is available separately.

items.t: Texas Instruments stock adds multiprotocol tools for factories
sum: Texas Instruments announced two industrial communication devices on Thursday, November 5, expanding its offering for factory automation, robotics and industrial Internet of Things systems. The company presented the products as a way to simplify connections across sensors, machines and control networks.

Morningstar, carrying the company release from PR Newswire, said the TICS100MOD is a multiprotocol communications system-on-module. It supports EtherCAT, EtherNet/IP and Profinet on one hardware platform, allowing engineers to switch protocols through a firmware update rather than redesigning the hardware.

The second product, the TIOM2212, is a dual-channel IO-Link master. It is designed to connect sensors and actuators with higher-level Industrial Ethernet networks and works with Texas Instruments' Sitara industrial networking system-on-chip family and AM13Ex real-time microcontrollers through an integrated frame handler. Texas Instruments said the approach can reduce design complexity and costs when linking field devices with factory control systems.

Preproduction quantities of the TIOM2212 are available through TI.com. The TICS100MOD is scheduled to become available by the end of 2026, giving customers access to the field-device component before the broader multiprotocol module reaches the market.

Texas Instruments will demonstrate the technology at electronica in Munich from Tuesday, November 10, through Friday, November 13. The demonstrations will focus on multiprotocol Industrial Ethernet, IO-Link, neural processing units and time-sensitive networking.

Texas Instruments stock traded at 253.15 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 15:42 CET on Friday, November 6, 2026, 3.12 percent below the Xetra close of Thursday, November 5. Investors will weigh the product expansion against the company's broader industrial and semiconductor demand outlook.

sum: Traders now price an 80% chance the Fed hikes again in December, and Treasuries yield more than every dividend stock on this list. Four income names have a record of thriving through tightening cycles, but each carries a risk worth…
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.

Although markets have enjoyed a strong run, with the benchmark S&P 500 up 12.45% year to date, the rate background has turned against income investors. Rate-setters raised rates at its September meeting, leaving the upper bound of the federal funds target at 4.00%. On Kalshi, a quarter-point hike at the December 9, 2026 meeting is priced at 80%, against 22% for a hold. But rising rates tend to rattle dividend stocks, because Treasuries and savings accounts start competing for the same income dollars. The 10-year Treasury yield is now at 4.95%, above the yield on every stock below.

The stocks that hold up typically share three traits: rising payouts, earnings that cover those payouts, and cash flow that funds buybacks too. During the last hiking cycle, from March 16, 2022, to July 26, 2023, all four names here finished higher. Automatic Data Processing (NASDAQ:ADP | ADP Price Prediction) jumped 22.36%, Texas Instruments (NASDAQ:TXN) gained 3.42%, Johnson & Johnson (NYSE:JNJ) rose 2.39%, and Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO) held flat at 0.04%. Each also raised its dividend during that span and during the 2015 to 2018 cycle. We highlighted income plays ahead of September’s Fed meeting, and the case for dividend growth has only strengthened since.

ADP pays $6.80 annually, a 2.24% yield at $304.02. Its $1.70 quarterly payout takes about 60% of fiscal Q1 2027 adjusted EPS of $2.82. Higher rates directly help: interest on client funds jumped 15% to $329.3 million as average balances grew to $36.9 billion. Management lifted fiscal 2027 adjusted EPS growth guidance to 10% to 12%. The quarterly dividend climbed from $1.04 to $1.25 across 2022, and from $0.63 to $0.79 during 2018. Risk: that float boost reverses once the Fed cuts, and payroll volumes track hiring.

Texas Instruments stock gains as Q3 revenue jumps 28%
sum: Texas Instruments reported strong third-quarter growth on October 21, 2026, as revenue advanced across its main end markets. The company's financial release shows revenue of 6.06 billion US dollars, net income of 2.43 billion US dollars and diluted earnings per share of 2.62 US dollars.

Revenue increased 28 percent from the third quarter of 2025 and 11 percent sequentially. Operating profit rose 73 percent to 2.87 billion US dollars, while net income increased 78 percent. Earnings per share rose 77 percent from 1.48 US dollars a year earlier.

Analog revenue grew 32 percent to 4.91 billion US dollars, and Embedded Processing revenue increased 21 percent to 858 million US dollars. Revenue in the company's other segment declined 6 percent to 286 million US dollars.

Management said industrial revenue increased more than 40 percent year over year and automotive revenue grew in the mid-teens. Data-center revenue rose about 95 percent year over year and 20 percent sequentially, according to the earnings-call transcript. The data-center business represented about 13 percent of third-quarter revenue.

Texas Instruments expects fourth-quarter revenue between 5.80 billion and 6.30 billion US dollars, with earnings per share between 2.45 and 2.79 US dollars. Management identified industrial, automotive and data-center markets as the main drivers of the outlook.

Chief Executive Haviv Ilan described data-center demand as strong and growing, with limited seasonal influence. He also pointed to increasing semiconductor content in industrial equipment and recovering automotive demand. The company is investing in manufacturing capacity to support higher output as demand broadens.

The third-quarter earnings release said trailing twelve-month operating cash flow reached 9.90 billion US dollars and non-GAAP free cash flow 8.42 billion US dollars. The free-cash-flow figure includes benefits related to the US CHIPS Act, so investors should distinguish the reported non-GAAP measure from operating cash flow.

items.t: What Could Texas Instruments Stock Be Worth In Three Years?
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Texas Instruments (TXN) stock returned 93.5% over the year to October 30, 2026, beating the 11.3% for the S&P 500. Investors are now paying 38.7 times its earnings over the last four fiscal quarters. That multiple sits above its average of 33.9 at the past twelve fiscal quarter ends. Whether you held through that run or watched it, how much more could the shares be worth if sales keep growing?

Under the scenario outlined below, Texas Instruments shares would be worth about $475.51 three years after the October 30 close. That compares to $300.84 that day, marking an upside of 58.1%, or 16.5% a year with dividends left out. The model assumes revenue grows 17.2% a year, set at 0.85 times its growth over the twelve months to fiscal Q3 2026. It sets the net margin at 70% of today’s figure plus 30% of its average at the twelve quarter ends before the latest one. The P/E stays at today’s level as an assumption rather than a forecast. This holds the multiple at 38.7 three years on, keeping it above the 33.9 average.

Higher sales supply all of the gain and a little more. A slightly lower net margin takes a little back, and the P/E adds nothing. Analog chips made up 79.2% of Texas Instruments’ sales in fiscal 2025. On the October 21 call, management said Analog revenue grew 32% from a year earlier in fiscal Q3 2026. By market, industrial sales rose more than 40%, and data center sales nearly doubled.

Management sees no slowdown, describing growing demand from industrial, automotive and data center customers. Revenue in fiscal Q3 2026 rose 27.7% from a year earlier, faster than the scenario’s pace. Part of that is a recovery. Management said industrial sales only now got back to their fiscal Q3 2022 level, four years later.

Texas Instruments is adding supply to keep up. Management said it can grow capacity every quarter, helped by a new site in Malaysia, and expects capital spending of $2 billion to $3 billion in 2026. Its only revenue guide covers one quarter, calling for $5.8 billion to $6.3 billion for fiscal Q4 2026. That range is centered at about the $6.06 billion reported for fiscal Q3, so it says nothing about a three-year pace.

What Comes Next For Texas Instruments After A 90% Gain
sum: If you had focused only on Texas Instruments' big AI data center headlines this year, it might be easy to forget a quieter but very concrete move. GE Appliances agreed to source one third of the chips for its new Kentucky laundry plant from TI, nearly doubling what it spends with the supplier. Holding Texas Instruments over the past year would have returned 89.9%, including dividends. If that decision sat on your desk back in October 2025, what exactly did you need to believe about TI’s industrial and automotive future to press “buy” before any of this news arrived?
The useful thing about a Narrative is that the reasoning is checkable: the assumptions sit beside the argument, and together they imply an estimated Fair Value you can disagree with.
Texas Instruments is not the only name tied to this theme. Zero in on 55 AI infrastructure stocks and compare how each one is priced.
The shares cost US$169 at the start of the period, and Texas Instruments sat between two very different but credible narratives about its future.

On the optimistic side, the October 2025 industrial and automotive thesis put fair value at US$206, which was 21% above the start price. That view rested on rising semiconductor content in factories and vehicles, as well as heavy U.S. 300mm fab investment that could strengthen supply security and support higher margins.

The May 2025 bear case pinned fair value at US$125, which was 26% below the start price. It focused on maturing analog and embedded markets, tougher Asian competitors, and rising compliance and capacity spending that could pressure margins and restrain free cash flow.

Texas Instruments’ Q3 2026 update showed revenue at US$6.06b versus US$4.74b a year earlier, with net income at US$2.41b versus US$1.36b. Net margin moved from 28.6% to 39.8%. That pattern supported the optimistic case that industrial, automotive, and data center demand could support higher profitability, although the planned Silicon Labs acquisition added future integration and financing questions.

Revenue is expected to range between $4.7 billion and $4.9 billion, with the $4.8 billion midpoint sitting well above the $4.56 billion consensus.

"Seagate delivered another quarter of record profitability and our highest ever free cash flow in the September quarter, demonstrating the earnings power of our business amid a strengthening demand environment," said Dave Mosley, Seagate's chair and chief executive officer.

Don't Overlook Texas Instruments (TXN) International Revenue Trends While Assessing the Stock
sum: Have you assessed how the international operations of Texas Instruments (TXN) performed in the quarter ended September 2026? For this chipmaker, possessing an expansive global footprint, parsing the trends of international revenues could be critical to gauge its financial resilience and growth prospects.

In today's increasingly interconnected global economy, a company's ability to tap into international markets can be a pivotal factor in shaping its overall financial health and growth trajectory. For investors, understanding a company's reliance on overseas markets has become increasingly crucial, as it offers insights into the company's sustainability of earnings, ability to tap into diverse economic cycles and overall growth potential.

Being present in foreign markets serves as protection against local economic declines and helps benefit from more rapidly expanding economies. Yet, such expansion also introduces challenges related to currency fluctuations, geopolitical uncertainties and varied market behaviors.

While delving into TXN's performance for the past quarter, we observed some fascinating trends in the revenue from its foreign segments that are commonly modeled and observed by analysts on Wall Street.

The recent quarter saw the company's total revenue reaching $6.06 billion, marking an improvement of 27.7% from the prior-year quarter. Next, we'll examine the breakdown of TXN's revenue from abroad to comprehend the significance of its international presence.

Of the total revenue, $104 million came from Rest of World during the last fiscal quarter, accounting for 1.7%. This represented a surprise of -5.62% as analysts had expected the region to contribute $110.19 million to the total revenue. In comparison, the region contributed $98 million, or 1.8%, and $74 million, or 1.6%, to total revenue in the previous and year-ago quarters, respectively.

During the quarter, Europe, Middle East and Africa contributed $1.21 billion in revenue, making up 19.9% of the total revenue. When compared to the consensus estimate of $1.24 billion, this meant a surprise of -2.52%. Looking back, Europe, Middle East and Africa contributed $1.08 billion, or 19.7%, in the previous quarter, and $972 million, or 20.5%, in the same quarter of the previous year.

Analog Semiconductors Stocks Q2 Recap: Benchmarking Analog Devices (NASDAQ:ADI)
sum: The end of the earnings season is always a good time to take a step back and see who shined (and who didn't). Let's take a look at how analog semiconductors stocks fared in Q2, starting with Analog Devices (NASDAQ:ADI).

Demand for analog chips is generally linked to the overall level of economic growth, as analog chips serve as the building blocks of most electronic goods and equipment. Unlike digital chip designers, analog chip makers tend to produce the majority of their own chips, as analog chip production does not require expensive leading edge nodes. Less dependent on major secular growth drivers, analog product cycles are much longer, often 5-7 years.
The 14 analog semiconductors stocks we track reported a very strong Q2. As a group, revenues beat analysts' consensus estimates by 1.8% while next quarter's revenue guidance was 4.9% above.
In light of this news, share prices of the companies have held steady as they are up 2.2% on average since the latest earnings results.

Founded by two MIT graduates, Ray Stata and Matthew Lorber in 1965, Analog Devices (NASDAQ:ADI) is one of the largest providers of high performance analog integrated circuits used mainly in industrial end markets, along with communications, autos, and consumer devices.

Analog Devices reported revenues of $4.02 billion, up 39.6% year on year. This print exceeded analysts' expectations by 2.6%. Overall, it was a very strong quarter for the company with revenue guidance for next quarter exceeding analysts' expectations and an impressive beat of analysts' operating income estimates.
"ADI delivered a strong third quarter, exceeding the midpoint of our revenue, margin, and earnings outlook as we capitalized on broad-based demand," said Vincent Roche, CEO and Chair.

sum: Now Live: Discover how much upside your favorite stocks could have using TIKR’s new Valuation Model (It’s free) >>>

Texas Instruments (TXN) has climbed about 60% in 2026, and for most of that run, the story was a simple demand rebound. On August 4, the company gave investors something more specific to hold onto. GE Appliances said it will source roughly one-third of the chips for its new Louisville laundry plant from Texas Instruments starting in 2027, a commitment that nearly doubles GE Appliances’ spending with the company.

GE chose Texas Instruments in part because it runs high-volume semiconductor fabs on U.S. soil, at a moment when supply chain security has become a boardroom priority. That is the advantage the market has been slow to price, and it is worth understanding before deciding whether a stock near $280 still has room to run.
Why a Washing Machine Contract Says Something About the Whole Company

The GE Appliances agreement is small next to Texas Instruments’ $19 billion in trailing revenue. Its value is what it confirms. GE runs a “Zero Distance” strategy built on shortening its supply chain, and it tied the decision to Texas Instruments’ domestic footprint, with chips coming from fabs in Sherman and Richardson, Texas, and Lehi, Utah. Production begins in 2027.

That is the same argument management made on the second-quarter earnings call, only from the customer’s side of the table. CEO Haviv Ilan described a market where TI’s inventory and capacity let it win business rivals cannot serve fast enough. “We are seeing examples, real-time examples of, hey, we are line down, please help us. And every time that happens, that’s an opportunity,” Ilan said. When a customer runs out of parts, the supplier that can ship becomes the supplier that keeps the design. A GE-sized commitment, negotiated years ahead of production, is the planned version of that same dynamic.

Texas Instruments plans to invest more than $60 billion across seven fabs in Texas and Utah, and the clean room space it built during the last downcycle now stands ready to absorb demand. Ilan called that readiness the difference between this cycle and the last one, when equipping a clean room took two to three years.

Operating margin is one of the best measures of profitability because it tells us how much money a company takes home after procuring and manufacturing its products, marketing and selling those products, and most importantly, keeping them relevant through research and development.

items.t: Texas Instruments Stock: Powering AI Beyond The GPU
sum: AI has pushed Texas Instruments (TXN) stock to near all-time highs, with shares surging roughly 70% year to date.

TI makes none of the AI compute chips everyone talks about, like Nvidia’s (NVDA ) GPUs and Broadcom’s (AVGO) custom chips. Instead, it builds analog and embedded processing chips: power management ICs, voltage regulators, and amplifiers, the unglamorous components that keep electronics running. For decades, this made TI a steady, cyclical industrial semiconductor company, the kind of name that moved with factory orders and auto production.

That’s changing. TI’s chips sit inside every AI server, regulating and distributing the enormous amounts of power modern GPUs consume. The market has taken notice, rewarding the stock with a forward earnings multiple of roughly 39x, rich for a company historically viewed as a slow-growth cyclical.

TI’s largest end market, industrial, is still recovering. Industrial revenue grew more than 30% year over year last quarter, marking eight straight quarters of sequential growth, yet the segment remains roughly 15% below its prior peak. That gap matters. A recovering cycle with room left to run supports a higher multiple than a business already at the top of its cycle. Earnings should continue to improve as the recovery unfolds. Management guided second-quarter revenue to $5.0 billion to $5.4 billion, well above analyst estimates, with growth expected across both industrial and data center markets.

Every AI server needs more than just GPUs, memory, and networking. It also requires a network of analog chips that convert, regulate, and monitor electricity, synchronize high-speed data flowing between processors and memory, and ensure the system operates reliably under heavy workloads. Without these components, the GPUs cannot be powered or communicate efficiently. As AI servers become larger and more power-intensive, the amount of analog content per server continues to increase.

TI has built the largest data center business in the analog semiconductor industry, generating approximately $1.5 billion in revenue in calendar 2025, up 64% year over year. Growth accelerated further in the first quarter of 2026, with data center revenue rising 90%, driven by demand for general-purpose amplifiers, clocking chips, and voltage references.

Furthermore, the investment narrative is increasingly supported by the company’s exposure to high-growth segments. The recent launch of its 800V DC power architecture highlights Texas Instruments' growing role in powering artificial intelligence data centers, which have yielded a surge in sequential revenue. This expansion into power solutions for high-performance computing, combined with early signs of recovery in the industrial and automotive markets, has mitigated concerns regarding capital expenditure drags and potential overcapacity from its domestic manufacturing buildout.

The stock is also benefiting from a structural index reclassification that took place in late June. Its removal from several defensive and value benchmarks and subsequent addition to the Russell 1000 Dynamic Index and the Russell Top 50 Index have altered its trading dynamics. This transition has brought fresh capital inflows from growth-focused institutional portfolios and passive ETFs, driving upward buying pressure and enhancing the stock's momentum.
